A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nonlinear system identification work, with the same underlying estimator and principal recovery guarantees. Their main text, figures, equations, and appendices provide readable material for comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-system simulations in Section 6 and Appendix C, measuring recovery under different disturbance probabilities, dimensions, and spectral norms.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulations in Section 8 and Appendix C, including revised existing experiments and additional rare-disturbance, sparse-matrix, and larger-system experiments.

M1.justification: The convex estimator and existing basis-function constructions remain unchanged. Section 7 adds an optional controller-driven excitation procedure: inject sparse, zero-mean Gaussian inputs when attacks provide insufficient exploration, with suggested target disturbance probabilities of 1/3 or 1/2. This extends data collection without changing the estimation objective.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic nonlinear system identification using bounded sine and Lipschitz radial basis functions. v3 extends the disturbance environment to rare and nearly absent disturbances, with p = 0.001, 0.1, and 0.3 in Appendix C.2. Larger dimensions and sparse system matrices are configurations within the retained task.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally compares the proposed estimator against another estimation method. v3 expands analytical discussion of least squares and related approaches, but its reported experiments still compare parameter settings of the same estimator.

E3.justification: The bounded-function probability sweep changes its stated horizon from T = 900 to 500, and the unstable-system stopping threshold changes from 10^15 to 10^14. New experiments introduce tridiagonal systems with T = 1000 and solves every 10 steps, and dimensions up to (50,100) with T = 1100 and solves every 100 steps. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2–C.4 adds analyses of inadequate excitation at small disturbance probabilities, recovery with sparse tridiagonal system matrices, and scalability to substantially larger systems. These test additional failure conditions and structural sensitivity. The original spectral-norm analysis is retained in Appendix C.1, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 independently generated trajectories per parameter setting and report averaged metrics. Neither provides experimental confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or seed values; the additional plots do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The five corresponding original plots contain revised numerical curves and convergence locations. New Figures 6–8 add results for rare disturbances, sparse matrices, and larger systems. Figure 6 reports failure to recover within 500 steps at p = 0.001 despite zero loss gap and optimality certificate, unlike recovery at p = 0.1 and 0.3. Changed experimental conditions prevent treating all plot differences as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v3 adds a nonidentifiability theorem concerning disturbances confined to a subspace, with a new argument in Appendix B.5. It also adds mathematical arguments about least-squares failure and excitation probabilities in Sections 4 and 7. The original optimality conditions, bounded/Lipschitz recovery bounds, and instability counterexample remain essentially unchanged under renumbering.

C1.justification: The central finite-time exact-recovery and sample-complexity claims remain. v3 adds faster learning through controller excitation to its stated contributions and reframes the headline scope as sparse disturbances or semi-oblivious attacks. The latter makes the existing conditional zero-mean-direction restriction more explicit rather than establishing a newly restricted theorem.

C2.justification: Sections 4 and 7 substantially expand interpretations of attack detectability, disturbance-driven exploration, and failure when disturbances are rare. New remarks discuss practical sample complexity and the tradeoff between basis regularity and approximation capacity; Appendix C.3 adds an implicit-regularization interpretation. Conversely, v1's explicit caveat that the evaluation metrics require unavailable ground truth and attacks is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3–C.4 adds concrete matrix-generation and computational details, including tridiagonal sparsity and optimization every 10 or 100 steps. Existing basis definitions, disturbance-generation recipes, and CVX usage were already documented in v1, largely in Appendix C, and are relocated into v3's main text. No code-release or hardware information is added.

R1.justification: v3 adds Wu et al. (2022), Kumar et al. (2022), and Moerland et al. (2023), with targeted discussion distinguishing system identification from robust reinforcement learning. It also expands the technical comparison with Yalcin et al. (2023). The existing system-identification and robust-regression literature, including the three comparison examples, is largely retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and disturbance/semi-oblivious terminology replaces much attack/stealth terminology. The literature review moves into the main text, optimality and uniqueness sections merge, and disturbance modeling and excitation receive separate sections. Experimental descriptions are reorganized between the main text and appendices.

P2.justification: Existing figures are redrawn with changed scales and plotting details. The bounded-function figures move from the appendix into the main text, while the spectral-norm figure moves into the appendix. Three additional figures include new two-panel displays. Typography, page geometry, headings, and the author block are also substantially reformatted.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful evidence about rare disturbances, sparse matrices, and larger systems, while clarifying the restricted attack model. However, the new Theorem 3 proof in Appendix B.5 incorrectly asserts that adding epsilon times the identity ensures diagonalizability, leaving its general reduction unjustified. With the principal recovery bounds unchanged, the empirical and explanatory gains coexist with a substantive new proof defect, making the net quality change unclear.
